items.title: Epoch AI shows open-weight GLM 5.3 turning public Firefox security patches into working exploits — Mozilla CTO responds with a coordination-across-layers strategy
items.summary: On October 29, 2026, Epoch AI published research showing that Z.ai's open-weight GLM 5.3 — which can be downloaded and run outside any provider's safety gate — was able to turn public Firefox security fixes into working browser exploits before users had a chance to install the patched build. Epoch tested six Firefox releases shipped between September 17 and October 26, 2026 (Firefox 156.0 through 158.0.1); the model successfully built a working exploit against every one of them, each chaining a patch-gap vulnerability (code execution inside Firefox's web content process, derived from a published fix that users had not yet installed) with a separate unpublished use-after-free that the model rediscovered on each run. The marginal cost per exploit was roughly $1,000 in API spend against total research spend of more than $100,000; 48-hour budget per attempt; fastest success 12 hours. Mozilla fixed the specific patch-gap bug in Firefox 159.0 (October 27, 2026) and Epoch has not yet confirmed whether the same chain still works against 159.0 but suspects the patch makes it substantially harder. At no point did GLM 5.3 trigger a safety refusal — the weights run locally, so no provider was in the loop to object. New overnight: Mozilla CTO Bobby Holley published a response on October 29 (expanded coverage in a November 4 French write-up from IT-Connect) describing a strategy to counter the patch gap. Mozilla's plan is to coordinate fixes across browser security layers so that gaps in different layers don't line up into a usable chain, and — per the IT-Connect account — to deliberately stagger when individual fixes land in public builds so an attacker can't read a single advisory and reconstruct the whole bug. Holley's framing is that closing the patch gap erodes an attacker's long-term advantage by making all discoveries cheap. Mozilla acknowledges the approach requires engineering coordination and may take time to implement; neither Mozilla nor Epoch has confirmed whether it's already in effect for Firefox 159.0 or will land in later releases. Epoch also said it plans to test more advanced open models and expects the threat to grow as capability rises — it specifically called out Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights planned for early November 2026, not yet tested) as a model that may outperform GLM 5.3 on offensive cyber tasks.
items.why_it_matters: This is the open-weight-world contrast to the GPT-6 Cyber story in today's morning section, and the Mozilla response that landed overnight is the part that turns it from a research demo into an ecosystem-level question. The OpenAI release is behind a gate: approved Daybreak Red customers only, with Preparedness Framework controls. GLM 5.3 has no such gate — the weights are public, the model runs locally, and Epoch's research is a working existence proof that an actor willing to spend roughly $1,000 per target can turn published Mozilla security fixes into usable browser exploits inside the window between patch publication and user install. The 'patch gap' used to be a human-attacker problem: a skilled vulnerability researcher could read an advisory and reconstruct the original bug, but that takes time, skill, and access, so most published patches were effectively safe once shipped. GLM 5.3's demonstration flattens that: patch publication has to be treated as a race against automated exploit generation. Mozilla's proposed answer — coordinating fixes across security layers so patch-gap bugs don't line up with other defects, and staggering when individual fixes land in public builds so attackers can't read one advisory and reconstruct the full chain — is an interesting trade-off to watch. It admits that the old 'ship fast, ship everything' security-update posture was calibrated for a slower threat and may need to change, and it also implies that users running patched builds get fixes staggered rather than all at once, which is a real cost. For Gabe's HTML/CSS/Python stack the direct relevance is twofold. First, auto-updating any browser you use for web development matters more now than it did last week. Second, the architectural pattern (open-weight model + agentic harness + patch diff as input + exploit as output) is a Python-stack project someone could build and defend against; it's a pure LLM-driven pipeline, not a specialized security tool. Over the next weeks the data points to watch: (1) whether stronger open models like Kimi K3.1 Pro can do the same thing to Chrome (Epoch's harness failed against Chrome on GLM 5.3 but noted that might not hold against a stronger model), and (2) whether Mozilla's coordination-across-layers strategy actually ships in a Firefox release, and what Chrome does — or doesn't — do in response.
items.why_it_matters_brief: An open-weight model built working Firefox exploits from public patches for ~$1,000 each, and Mozilla's response is to coordinate fixes across security layers so patch-gap bugs stop lining up — patch publication is now a race against automated exploit generation.

items.title: A tampered Claude Code extension sat on Cursor's marketplace for 11 hours — SSH backdoor payload mostly failed without admin privileges, but recon and persistence files still landed, and Cursor's remediation guide says updating isn't enough
items.summary: On October 29, 2026, Cursor disclosed that a maliciously modified copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension — published under the legitimate Anthropic.claude-code name at versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and macOS — was available in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace for roughly 11 hours (approximately 2:27 AM to 1:35 PM Pacific Time). Cursor puts the exposure at up to 5,000 users. The payload was designed to add an unauthorized SSH key labeled 'svc-telemetry' to authorized_keys, enable the local SSH service, drop startup scripts that live outside the extension directory, and open a reverse SSH tunnel. New overnight clarification: Cursor's own notice and follow-up security coverage confirm that the SSH-enabling step mostly failed in practice because of errors in the malicious code and standard Windows/macOS permission prompts — on most installs it required Cursor to have been launched with administrator privileges to succeed. Recon still ran on load (host and user information collection) and the persistence files were still written in some runs, so the 'how exposed am I' answer depends on whether the extension was active and whether Cursor was run elevated during the window. Anthropic published a clean 2.1.314 to both Open VSX and the Microsoft VS Code Marketplace, but Cursor and multiple security outlets explicitly warn that updating to 2.1.314 does not undo earlier compromise — a developer who ran 2.1.313 still needs to check for the svc-telemetry SSH key, remove it, look for added startup scripts and persistence hooks, and rotate credentials and sessions from a trusted system. Cursor's npm package and the Microsoft VS Code Marketplace copy of the extension were not affected — the compromise was confined to Cursor's marketplace distribution. New overnight on attribution: security researchers Beaumont and Phorion said the tampered build was distributed through Anthropic's official publisher account on Cursor; Cursor's own public notice says the build was not developed by Anthropic and describes the incident as a malicious actor using access to Cursor's marketplace to publish under the Anthropic.claude-code name. Anthropic has said a malicious actor used marketplace access to publish a tampered copy that Anthropic did not build or publish, and that there is no evidence Anthropic's own systems or official distribution channels were compromised. Cursor has not publicly identified the attacker or said how the publishing credentials were obtained. Cursor is owned by SpaceX as of an earlier 2026 acquisition.
items.why_it_matters: This is a supply-chain story disguised as an AI-tools story, and the interesting thing about it is where the trust boundary actually was — plus the overnight clarifications on what the payload actually managed to do. Developers who installed the Claude Code extension through Cursor's marketplace reasonably expected the Anthropic.claude-code package to be the same code Anthropic publishes to the Microsoft VS Code Marketplace — the publisher name is Anthropic's, the version numbers match, and there's nothing in the install flow that distinguishes a vetted copy from a marketplace mirror. What the attackers exploited was that Cursor runs its own marketplace (not Microsoft's VS Code Marketplace, which is proprietary to Microsoft and license-restricted for forks) and that marketplace apparently accepted a publisher identity it should not have — the Beaumont/Phorion claim that distribution happened via Anthropic's official account is in open dispute with Cursor's own account that the attacker used marketplace access to publish under Anthropic's name, and neither side has explained how the account or marketplace access was obtained. The architectural detail matters for anyone using any VS Code fork: Cursor, Windsurf, and Google Antigravity all ship their own extension marketplaces or default to Open VSX, which is a separate registry from Microsoft's with different publisher-verification guarantees. The overnight clarification on payload execution is the practical one: the SSH-backdoor install step mostly fails without admin privileges, so most normal installs (Cursor launched without elevation) would have had the recon run and some files drop but not get the live SSH tunnel. That is not the same as 'you're fine' — the persistence scripts can land, and recon ran regardless. For Gabe's practical setup — HTML/CSS/Python, likely using VS Code or a fork for editing — the useful questions are which editor's marketplace you install extensions from, whether you occasionally spot-check what a popular extension's publisher name actually points to, and whether you ever launch your editor elevated. The persistence detail remains important even with the admin-privilege softening: the payload wrote files outside the extension directory specifically so that uninstalling the extension doesn't clean up. Checking ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for 'svc-telemetry' and reviewing shell startup scripts is still the right move for anyone who ran Cursor on October 29.
items.why_it_matters_brief: A tampered Claude Code extension shipped under Anthropic's name through Cursor's marketplace for 11 hours — the SSH-backdoor step mostly failed without admin privileges, but recon ran and persistence files still landed, so updating to the clean 2.1.314 doesn't clean up the earlier run.

items.title: Google DeepMind's AI agents compressed months of cryptanalysis into weeks — two new weaknesses found in legacy 1024-bit RSA, modern keys unaffected
items.summary: On November 6, 2026, Google DeepMind announced that AI agents, working alongside cryptanalysts Nadia Heninger (UC San Diego) and Emmanuel Thomé (Inria), found two new cryptographic advances against legacy 1024-bit RSA systems — going beyond what the same researchers accomplished in a September 2026 academic paper using traditional CPU methods alone. The first finding makes forging signatures on short-digest 1024-bit RSA roughly 1,600x more efficient than prior approaches. The second cuts the average cost of factoring each additional 1024-bit key by about 30x compared with previously known batch methods. DeepMind VP Pushmeet Kohli described the work as completing in a matter of weeks — in contrast to the September 2026 paper by Heninger, Thomé, and three co-authors (IACR ePrint 2026/2131), which required approximately 1,380 CPU core-years over five months using traditional implementation, and explicitly noted that it used no AI tools. DeepMind's AI agents reproduced and extended those results faster by guiding the combinatorial search. The research was led inside DeepMind by Dj Dvijotham and Abhradeep Thakurta. Neither finding affects RSA-2048 or larger keys; 1024-bit RSA has been banned for new deployments under NIST guidance since 2013. No production systems using modern key sizes are at risk from either result.
items.why_it_matters: The cryptographic content of this announcement matters less than the meta-point about research velocity. The underlying 1024-bit RSA weaknesses are real but affect a class of keys NIST has disallowed since 2013. The interesting signal is what DeepMind is demonstrating about AI-accelerated domain-expert research. The September 2026 academic paper by the same cryptanalysts took 1,380 CPU core-years over five months to forge a 1024-bit RSA signature without factoring the key — and the paper itself notes it used no AI or GPU acceleration. DeepMind's follow-up used AI agents to push beyond that baseline, finding the batch-factoring speedup and the 1,600x signature-forgery efficiency gain, in weeks. That's the threshold-moment framing: not 'AI broke encryption' (it did not, modern keys are fine), but 'AI is now usefully compressing specialized cryptographic research that previously required months of expert CPU time.' The practical relevance for Gabe is two-part. First, any system still using 1024-bit RSA — and there are more than you'd expect in legacy APIs, HSM configurations, and embedded devices — should be treated as imminently compromisable, not just theoretically deprecated. Second, the AI-guided-expert-researcher pattern (humans set the goal, AI agents do the combinatorial search, humans validate the result) is becoming a credible methodology in a domain — cryptanalysis — that was previously human-expert-only. That same pattern is showing up in Epoch AI's Firefox exploit research (GLM 5.3 in this morning's other Tier 1 item), and it's likely to show up next in chemistry, materials science, and software verification. When two independent teams (Epoch's AI-generated Firefox exploits, DeepMind's AI-assisted cryptanalysis) publish AI-accelerated results in the same week that previously took human researchers months or years, the signal is that the research acceleration pattern is not a one-off.
items.why_it_matters_brief: AI agents compressed months of expert cryptanalysis into weeks — a 1,600x signature-forgery speedup on legacy 1024-bit RSA; RSA-2048 is fine, but the AI-guided research acceleration pattern is the actual signal here.

items.title: Moonshot AI releases Kimi K3.1 Pro weights — 2.8T MoE, 1M context, ranks 4th on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index; Epoch AI named it the open-weight model most likely to extend the Firefox patch-gap result to Chrome
items.summary: Moonshot AI shipped the open weights for Kimi K3.1 Pro on November 4–5, 2026, meeting the commitment made at the API launch on October 23. The model is a 2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts with 104B active parameters per token, a 1M-token context window, and multimodal input (text and images). Weights are on Hugging Face at moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro as 96 safetensors files totaling about 1.56 TB, distributed in MXFP4 precision; vLLM, SGLang, and TokenSpeed are the recommended serving frameworks. At launch the model ranked 4th on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (scoring 55.1, behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 57.6 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 56.0), placed 3rd on the GDPval-AA agentic benchmark (1,846 Elo, behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 1,866 and Muse Wonder Full at 1,857), and scored 67% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 64%). On Moonshot's own BenchCAD benchmark for 3D parametric modeling it scores 92.7% with tools, close to Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2%) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9%). Moonshot's kimi.com blog reports the model on WebDev Arena at 1,691 points (8th, level with Claude Opus 5). The license is Moonshot's 'Kimi K3.1 Pro License' — MIT-style rights to use, modify, and fine-tune the weights for most users, with additional revenue-sharing conditions for large commercial model-as-a-service deployments. Epoch AI called out Kimi K3.1 Pro specifically in their October 29 Firefox patch-gap research as the open-weight model they most expect to extend the GLM 5.3 result to Chrome; GLM 5.3's harness failed against Chrome, and Epoch said stronger open models might change that.
items.why_it_matters: Two threads worth pulling apart. The first is performance positioning: a 4th-place finish on Artificial Analysis's composite benchmark for an open-weight model under a modified-MIT license is a meaningful data point in the open-vs-closed capability gap. Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 are still ahead on composite scoring, but the gap has closed relative to Kimi K3 — the agentic benchmark result (3rd at 1,846 Elo) puts K3.1 Pro in a tier that until recently was proprietary-model territory. For Gabe's Python work, the practical angle is that the 2.8T total / 104B active MoE architecture is not a laptop runner — 1.56TB of weights means data-center infrastructure — but the 104B-active figure means inference cost is closer to a 100B-class dense model than to a 2.8T dense model. At 2-bit quantization, running this on rented GPU instances is feasible; full fine-tuning is not, but LoRA on specific tasks probably is. The second thread is the Epoch AI connection in this morning's other Tier 1 item. Epoch's October 29 Firefox patch-gap research explicitly named Kimi K3.1 Pro as the next open-weight model likely to push the result further — specifically, they noted GLM 5.3's harness failed against Chrome and suggested that a stronger open model might change that. The weights are now publicly available on Hugging Face. That's the item worth watching: not whether Moonshot's self-reported benchmarks are accurate, but whether anyone reproduces the Epoch harness against Chrome with Kimi K3.1 Pro over the next few weeks. If that test succeeds, the patch-gap attack pattern moves from 'Firefox only' to 'both major desktop browsers,' and the ecosystem response question gets considerably more urgent.
